subject: bnss
question: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, came into force on:
explanation: The BNSS came into force on 1 July 2024 by Central Government notification under Section 1(3), together with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. Section 531 repeals the CrPC, 1973, while saving appeals, applications, trials, inquiries and investigations pending on that date, which continue under the old Code.

subject: bnss
question: Information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence (the First Information Report) is recorded by the officer in charge of a police station under which section of the BNSS?
explanation: Section 173 of the BNSS governs information in cognizable cases and corresponds to Section 154 of the CrPC. Section 175 (old Section 156) deals with the power to investigate, Section 180 (old Section 161) with examination of witnesses, and Section 193 (old Section 173) with the final police report.

subject: bnss
question: The power of a police officer making an investigation to examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts of the case is found in:
explanation: Section 180 of the BNSS (old Section 161 CrPC) allows the investigating officer to examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case and to reduce the statement to writing. Section 181 (old Section 162) restricts the use of such statements, and Section 179 (old Section 160) deals with requiring the attendance of witnesses.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 58 of the BNSS, a police officer shall not detain in custody a person arrested without warrant for longer than ______, exclusive of the time necessary for the journey to the Magistrate's court, without a Magistrate's order.
explanation: Section 58 of the BNSS (old Section 57 CrPC) bars detention of a person arrested without warrant beyond twenty-four hours, exclusive of journey time to the Magistrate's court, in the absence of a special order under Section 187. It gives effect to the guarantee in Article 22(2) of the Constitution.

subject: bnss
question: An order for maintenance of wives, children and parents is made by a Magistrate under:
explanation: Section 144 of the BNSS provides for orders of maintenance of wives, children and parents and corresponds to Section 125 of the CrPC. Section 163 of the BNSS (old Section 144 CrPC) deals with urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger, so the old and new numbers must not be confused.

subject: bnss
question: A direction for the grant of bail to a person apprehending arrest for a non-bailable offence (anticipatory bail) is given under:
explanation: Section 482 of the BNSS empowers the High Court or Court of Session to grant anticipatory bail and corresponds to Section 438 of the CrPC. Section 478 (old 436) covers bail in bailable offences, Section 480 (old 437) bail in non-bailable offences, and Section 483 (old 439) the special powers of the High Court and Court of Session regarding bail.

subject: bnss
question: The saving of the inherent powers of the High Court to make orders necessary to give effect to any order under the Sanhita, prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise secure the ends of justice is in:
explanation: Section 528 of the BNSS saves the inherent powers of the High Court and corresponds to Section 482 of the CrPC. Section 482 of the BNSS now deals with anticipatory bail, Section 530 with trials and proceedings in electronic mode, and Section 531 with repeal and savings.

subject: bnss
question: Bail as of right for a person accused of a bailable offence is provided in:
explanation: Section 478 of the BNSS (old Section 436 CrPC) provides that a person accused of a bailable offence who is arrested or detained without warrant and is prepared to give bail shall be released on bail. Section 479 (old 436A) deals with the maximum period of detention of undertrial prisoners.

subject: bnss
question: Confessions and statements are recorded by a Judicial Magistrate in the course of an investigation under:
explanation: Section 183 of the BNSS (old Section 164 CrPC) empowers a Judicial Magistrate to record confessions and statements during investigation, after warning the person that he is not bound to confess and that the confession may be used against him. The BNSS allows the confession or statement to be recorded by audio-video electronic means in the presence of the accused's advocate.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 173(1) of the BNSS, information about a cognizable offence may be given to the officer in charge of a police station:
options: only if the offence was committed within the limits of that police station
irrespective of the area where the offence was committed
only after a Magistrate's permission when the offence occurred elsewhere
only in writing and in person
explanation: Section 173(1) of the BNSS allows information relating to a cognizable offence to be given irrespective of the area where the offence is committed, giving statutory form to the "zero FIR". The old Section 154 CrPC contained no such words, though courts had recognised the practice; the FIR is then transferred to the police station having jurisdiction.

subject: bnss
question: Where information about a cognizable offence is given by electronic communication under Section 173(1)(ii) of the BNSS, it shall be taken on record on being signed by the informant within:
explanation: Section 173(1)(ii) of the BNSS provides that information given by electronic communication shall be taken on record by the officer on being signed within three days by the person giving it. The provision on e-FIRs is new; the old Section 154 CrPC dealt only with oral and written information.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 173(3) of the BNSS, for a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of three years or more but less than seven years, the officer in charge may, with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, conduct a preliminary enquiry to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists within:
explanation: Section 173(3) of the BNSS permits, for offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, either a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days to ascertain a prima facie case, or immediate investigation, with the prior permission of a DSP-rank officer. Section 154 of the CrPC contained no statutory provision for a preliminary enquiry.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 176(3) of the BNSS, for every offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more, the officer in charge of the police station shall, from a date notified by the State Government, cause:
options: the accused to be produced before the Sessions Judge
a forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence and the process to be videographed
the case to be transferred to the CID
a Judicial Magistrate to supervise the investigation
explanation: Section 176(3) of the BNSS makes a forensic expert's visit to the crime scene and videography of the process mandatory for offences punishable with seven years or more, from a date the State Government notifies within five years. Section 176 otherwise corresponds to Section 157 of the CrPC (procedure for investigation).

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 187(3) of the BNSS, the maximum total period for which a Magistrate may authorise detention of an accused during investigation, where the offence is punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years or more, is:
explanation: Section 187(3) of the BNSS (old Section 167(2) CrPC) limits detention during investigation to ninety days where the offence is punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of ten years or more, and sixty days for any other offence. On expiry, the accused is entitled to be released on bail if prepared to furnish it (default bail).

subject: bnss
question: A Magistrate empowered under Section 210 of the BNSS may order an investigation into a cognizable case under Section 175(3), after considering an application supported by:
options: a certificate from the Public Prosecutor
a report from the Superintendent of Police alone
explanation: Section 175(3) of the BNSS (old Section 156(3) CrPC) allows the Magistrate to order investigation after considering an application supported by an affidavit under Section 173(4), after such inquiry as he thinks necessary and after considering the submission of the police officer. Section 173(4) applies where the officer in charge has refused to record the information and the Superintendent of Police has not acted on it.

subject: bnss
question: Under the first proviso to Section 223(1) of the BNSS, a Magistrate shall not take cognizance of an offence on a complaint:
options: without examining at least two witnesses
without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard
without the sanction of the Sessions Judge
explanation: Section 223 of the BNSS (old Section 200 CrPC) requires the Magistrate to examine the complainant and witnesses on oath, and its first proviso adds that no cognizance shall be taken without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard. That pre-cognizance hearing is new; the CrPC did not require it.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 218 of the BNSS, where the Government fails to decide a request for sanction to prosecute a public servant within the prescribed period, sanction is deemed to have been accorded. That period is:
explanation: Section 218 of the BNSS (old Section 197 CrPC) requires previous sanction to prosecute judges and public servants for acts done in discharge of official duty. Its new proviso requires the Government to decide within one hundred and twenty days of receiving the request, failing which sanction is deemed to have been accorded.

subject: bnss
question: Where arrest is not required under Section 35(1) of the BNSS, the police officer shall issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made to appear before him. This notice of appearance corresponds to which provision of the old CrPC?
explanation: Section 35(3) to (6) of the BNSS carry forward the notice of appearance under Section 41A of the CrPC. Where the person complies with the notice and continues to comply, he shall not be arrested unless, for reasons recorded, the officer is of the opinion that he ought to be arrested; Section 35 as a whole corresponds to Section 41 of the CrPC.

subject: bnss
question: The duty of a police officer arresting a person without warrant to communicate the full particulars of the offence or other grounds of arrest, and to inform a person not accused of a non-bailable offence of the right to bail, is in:
explanation: Section 47 of the BNSS (old Section 50 CrPC) requires the arresting officer to communicate forthwith the full particulars of the offence or other grounds of arrest, and to inform a person arrested for an offence other than a non-bailable offence that he is entitled to be released on bail. Section 48 (old Section 50A) requires information about the arrest to be given to a nominated person.

subject: bnss
question: An order by an Executive Magistrate in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger under Section 163 of the BNSS shall not, unless extended by the State Government, remain in force for more than:
explanation: Section 163(4) of the BNSS (old Section 144(4) CrPC) limits such an order to two months from the making of it. Under the proviso, the State Government may, if it considers it necessary for preventing danger to human life, health or safety or a riot, extend it by notification for up to six months from the date the Magistrate's order would otherwise have expired.

subject: bnss
question: The compounding of offences, listing which offences may be compounded with or without the permission of the court, is governed by:
explanation: Section 359 of the BNSS (old Section 320 CrPC) sets out the offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita that may be compounded by the specified persons, some without and some only with the court's permission. A composition has the effect of an acquittal (Section 359(8)); Section 360 (old 321) deals with withdrawal from prosecution.

subject: bnss
question: Under the proviso to Section 413 of the BNSS, the victim has a right to prefer an appeal against an order of the court:
options: acquitting the accused, convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation
explanation: Section 413 of the BNSS (old Section 372 CrPC) provides that no appeal lies except as provided by the Sanhita or any other law. Its proviso gives the victim a right to appeal against an order acquitting the accused, convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation, to the court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against a conviction.

subject: bnss
question: Section 398 of the BNSS requires every State Government to:
options: establish a special court for witness intimidation
prepare and notify a Witness Protection Scheme for the State
pay travel allowance to all witnesses
record the evidence of all witnesses by video conferencing
explanation: Section 398 of the BNSS directs every State Government to prepare and notify a Witness Protection Scheme for the State with a view to ensuring the protection of witnesses. The CrPC had no corresponding provision.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 105 of the BNSS, the process of conducting a search and seizure, including preparing the list of seized items and its signing by witnesses, shall be:
options: recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably a mobile phone, and forwarded without delay to the Magistrate
conducted only in the presence of a Judicial Magistrate
recorded only in the case diary
conducted only between sunrise and sunset
explanation: Section 105 of the BNSS, which has no equivalent in the CrPC, requires search and seizure under Chapter VII or Section 185 to be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably a mobile phone. The police officer must forward the recording without delay to the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

subject: bnss
question: Under the proviso to Section 479(1) of the BNSS, an undertrial prisoner who is a first-time offender (never convicted of any offence) shall be released on bond by the court if he has undergone detention for up to:
options: one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment for the offence
one-fourth of the maximum period of imprisonment for the offence
two-thirds of the maximum period of imprisonment for the offence
one-third of the maximum period of imprisonment for the offence
explanation: Section 479(1) of the BNSS (old Section 436A CrPC) entitles an undertrial, other than one accused of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, to release on bail after detention for one-half of the maximum term. Its new proviso reduces this to one-third for a first-time offender, and Section 479(2) bars such release where investigation, inquiry or trial is pending in more than one offence.

flags.note: New first-time-offender proviso in Section 479 BNSS; confirm wording.
The Supreme Court (In re Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons, 2024) applied this proviso to undertrials whose cases began before 1 July 2024. Check whether it should be mentioned.

subject: bnss
question: Section 356 of the BNSS, which has no counterpart in the CrPC, permits:
options: the trial of a proclaimed offender who has absconded to evade trial, in his absence, as if he were present
the trial of a juvenile by a Court of Session
the summary trial of all offences punishable up to seven years
the transfer of a trial to a court outside India
explanation: Section 356 of the BNSS provides for inquiry, trial and judgment in absentia where a person declared a proclaimed offender has absconded to evade trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him; this is deemed a waiver of his right to be present. Safeguards include notices and the appointment of an advocate for his defence; the CrPC (Section 299) only allowed evidence to be recorded in the absence of the accused.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 23 of the BNSS, a Judicial Magistrate of the first class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or of fine not exceeding ______, or both, or of community service.
explanation: Section 23(2) of the BNSS (old Section 29(2) CrPC) raises the fine a Judicial Magistrate of the first class may impose from ten thousand to fifty thousand rupees, and adds community service as a sentence. A Judicial Magistrate of the second class may impose up to one year's imprisonment, a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or community service (Section 23(3)).

flags.note: Confirm the fine limits in Section 23(2) and (3) BNSS (Rs. 50,000 and Rs. 10,000) against the bare act.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 187(2) and (3) of the BNSS, police custody of an accused during investigation may be authorised for a total not exceeding fifteen days, which:
options: must be taken only within the first fifteen days after arrest, as under the CrPC
may be taken in whole or in parts at any time during the initial forty or sixty days of the sixty- or ninety-day detention period
may be taken at any time until the charge-sheet is filed, without limit
may be extended to thirty days with the Sessions Judge's approval
explanation: Section 187 of the BNSS (old Section 167 CrPC) allows police custody of up to fifteen days in the whole or in parts at any time during the initial forty days or sixty days out of the sixty- or ninety-day detention period. Under the CrPC, as read in CBI v. Anupam J. Kulkarni (1992), police custody was confined to the first fifteen days after production.

flags.note: New split-custody rule in Section 187 BNSS; confirm wording.
Mentions CBI v. Anupam J. Kulkarni (1992). Courts are still interpreting the new provision.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 35(7) of the BNSS, no arrest shall be made without the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police where the offence is punishable with imprisonment for less than three years and the person is:
options: infirm or above sixty years of age
explanation: Section 35(7) of the BNSS is a new safeguard requiring the prior permission of a DSP-rank officer before arresting a person who is infirm or above sixty years of age for an offence punishable with less than three years' imprisonment. The rest of Section 35 carries forward Sections 41 and 41A of the CrPC on arrest without warrant and notice of appearance.

subject: bnss
question: Section 107 of the BNSS, which has no counterpart in the CrPC, empowers the Magistrate, on the application of a police officer, to:
options: order the attachment, forfeiture or restoration of property believed to be derived directly or indirectly from criminal activity
issue a look-out circular against an absconding accused
order the demolition of illegal structures used in crime
explanation: Section 107 of the BNSS allows a Magistrate, on the application of an investigating police officer with the approval of the Superintendent or Commissioner of Police, to attach property reasonably believed to be proceeds of crime, after hearing the person concerned. The Magistrate may later order distribution of the proceeds to persons affected by the crime; the CrPC had no comparable power outside special laws.

flags.note: New provision in Section 107 BNSS; confirm the rank of approving officer and the procedure described.

subject: bnss
question: The report of the police officer on completion of investigation, forwarded to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance, is governed by:
explanation: Section 193 of the BNSS (old Section 173 CrPC) requires every investigation to be completed without unnecessary delay and the officer in charge to forward a report to the Magistrate in the prescribed form. Section 210 (old Section 190) deals with the Magistrate's cognizance on such a report.

subject: bnss
question: Where a court has reason to believe that a person against whom a warrant has been issued has absconded or is concealing himself, it may publish a written proclamation requiring him to appear under:
explanation: Section 84 of the BNSS (old Section 82 CrPC) provides for a proclamation for a person absconding, requiring him to appear at a specified place and time. Section 85 (old Section 83) allows attachment of his property, and Section 94 (old Section 91) deals with summons to produce documents.

subject: bnss
question: A court or the officer in charge of a police station may issue a summons or written order to a person to produce a document or other thing necessary for an investigation, inquiry or trial under:
explanation: Section 94 of the BNSS (old Section 91 CrPC) empowers a court, or an officer in charge of a police station, to summon a person to produce any document, electronic communication or other thing whose production is necessary or desirable for any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding. The BNSS expressly includes digital evidence and electronic communication devices.

subject: bnss
question: The revisional powers of the High Court in criminal cases, corresponding to Section 401 of the CrPC, are now found in:
explanation: Section 442 of the BNSS (old Section 401 CrPC) sets out the High Court's powers of revision. Section 438 (old Section 397) empowers the High Court and Sessions Judge to call for and examine the record of an inferior criminal court, and Section 528 (old Section 482) saves the High Court's inherent powers.

subject: bnss
question: Appeals from convictions, for example from a conviction on a trial held by a Sessions Judge to the High Court, are provided for in:
explanation: Section 415 of the BNSS (old Section 374 CrPC) provides for appeals from convictions, including an appeal to the High Court from a conviction on a trial held by a Sessions Judge. Section 413 (old Section 372) states that no appeal lies except as provided, and Section 419 (old Section 378) deals with appeals against acquittal.

subject: bnss
question: Which section of the BNSS provides that trials, inquiries and proceedings, including the issue, service and execution of summons and warrants and the recording of evidence, may be held in electronic mode?
explanation: Section 530 of the BNSS allows all trials, inquiries and proceedings under the Sanhita, including service of summons and warrants, examination of complainants and witnesses, recording of evidence and appellate proceedings, to be held in electronic mode by electronic communication or audio-video electronic means. The CrPC had no equivalent general provision.

subject: bnss
question: A police officer who knows of a design to commit a cognizable offence may arrest the person so designing, without orders from a Magistrate and without a warrant, if the commission of the offence cannot otherwise be prevented. This preventive arrest is under:
explanation: Section 170 of the BNSS (old Section 151 CrPC) permits arrest to prevent the commission of a cognizable offence where it appears to the officer that the offence cannot otherwise be prevented. Under Section 170(2), such a person shall not be detained for more than twenty-four hours from the arrest unless further detention is required or authorised under the Sanhita or any other law.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 181 of the BNSS, a statement made by any person to a police officer in the course of an investigation, if reduced to writing:
options: shall be signed by the person making it
shall be read over and countersigned by a Magistrate
shall not be signed by the person making it
is admissible as substantive evidence at the trial
explanation: Section 181(1) of the BNSS (old Section 162 CrPC) provides that no statement made to a police officer in the course of investigation shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it. Such a statement may be used only to contradict the witness at the trial in the manner provided by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, not as substantive evidence.

subject: bnss
question: The power of a police officer to arrest without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, corresponding to Section 41 of the CrPC, is found in:
explanation: Section 35 of the BNSS (old Section 41 CrPC) lists when a police officer may arrest without warrant, for example a person who commits a cognizable offence in his presence. Section 43 (old Section 46) deals with how an arrest is made, Section 47 (old Section 50) with informing the grounds of arrest, and Section 58 (old Section 57) with the 24-hour limit.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 193(3)(ii) of the BNSS, the police officer must inform the informant or the victim of the progress of the investigation, by any means including electronic communication, within:
explanation: Section 193(3)(ii) of the BNSS requires the police officer, within ninety days, to inform the informant or the victim of the progress of the investigation, by any means including electronic communication. The old Section 173 CrPC only required the action taken to be communicated to the informant after the final report.

subject: bnss
question: Under the proviso to Section 193(9) of the BNSS, further investigation during the trial may be conducted with the permission of the court trying the case and shall be completed within:
options: thirty days, which cannot be extended
ninety days, which may be extended with the permission of the court
six months, which may be extended by the High Court
one year from the date of the charge-sheet
explanation: Section 193(9) of the BNSS (old Section 173(8) CrPC) preserves the power of further investigation after a report is forwarded. Its new proviso requires further investigation during the trial to be conducted with the permission of the trial court and completed within ninety days, extendable with the court's permission.

flags.note: New proviso to Section 193(9) BNSS on further investigation during trial; confirm the 90-day limit and the subsection number.

subject: bnss
question: In a case committed to the Court of Session, the accused may prefer an application for discharge under Section 250(1) of the BNSS within:
options: sixty days from the date of commitment
thirty days from the date of commitment
ninety days from the date of commitment
sixty days from the framing of charge
explanation: Section 250(1) of the BNSS (old Section 227 CrPC) allows the accused to apply for discharge within sixty days from the date of commitment of the case under Section 232. If the judge considers that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall discharge the accused, recording his reasons (Section 250(2)).

subject: bnss
question: Where a Sessions Judge is of opinion that there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the charge shall be framed under Section 251(1)(b) of the BNSS within:
options: sixty days from the date of first hearing on charge
thirty days from the date of commitment
fourteen days from supply of documents
ninety days from the filing of the police report
explanation: Section 251(1)(b) of the BNSS (old Section 228(1)(b) CrPC) requires the charge to be framed in writing within sixty days from the date of the first hearing on charge. The charge is then read and explained to the accused, who is asked whether he pleads guilty or claims to be tried (Section 251(2)).

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 258 of the BNSS, after hearing arguments in a sessions trial, the Judge shall give judgment within ______ from the completion of arguments, which may be extended for reasons recorded in writing to ______.
explanation: Section 258 of the BNSS (old Section 235 CrPC) requires the judgment in a sessions trial to be given as soon as possible, within thirty days from the date of completion of arguments, extendable to forty-five days for reasons to be recorded in writing. The CrPC prescribed no time limit for pronouncing judgment.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 283(1) of the BNSS, a Chief Judicial Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class shall try summarily a case of theft where the value of the property stolen does not exceed:
explanation: Section 283(1) of the BNSS (old Section 260 CrPC) makes summary trial mandatory for listed offences, including theft where the value of the property stolen does not exceed twenty thousand rupees (the CrPC limit was two thousand rupees). Section 283(2) also allows a Magistrate, after hearing the accused, to try summarily offences punishable with imprisonment up to three years.

flags.note: Confirm the Rs. 20,000 value limit and the mandatory 'shall' in Section 283(1) BNSS against the bare act.

subject: bnss
question: An accused who wishes to avail of plea bargaining under Chapter XXIII of the BNSS must file the application within:
options: thirty days from the date of framing of charge
sixty days from the date of filing of the police report
fifteen days from the first appearance
explanation: Section 290(1) of the BNSS requires the application for plea bargaining to be filed within thirty days from the date of framing of charge; the CrPC (Section 265B) fixed no such time limit. Plea bargaining remains unavailable for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment exceeding seven years, and for offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country.

subject: bnss
question: After issuing a proclamation for a person absconding, the court may order the attachment of any movable or immovable property belonging to the proclaimed person under:
explanation: Section 85 of the BNSS (old Section 83 CrPC) empowers the court issuing a proclamation under Section 84 to order attachment of the proclaimed person's movable or immovable property, for reasons recorded in writing. The attachment may be ordered at the same time as the proclamation if the person is about to dispose of or remove his property.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 230 of the BNSS, in a case instituted on a police report, the Magistrate shall furnish copies of the police report and other documents to the accused and the victim (if represented by an advocate) without delay and in no case beyond:
options: seven days from the production or appearance of the accused
fourteen days from the production or appearance of the accused
thirty days from the filing of the charge-sheet
sixty days from the date of cognizance
explanation: Section 230 of the BNSS (old Section 207 CrPC) requires the Magistrate to supply copies of the police report, FIR, statements and other documents without delay, and in no case beyond fourteen days from the date of production or appearance of the accused. It also extends the supply to the victim represented by an advocate and allows supply in electronic form.

subject: bnss
question: In a warrant case instituted on a police report, the accused may apply for discharge under Section 262(1) of the BNSS within:
options: thirty days from the date of cognizance
ninety days from the date of the first hearing
sixty days from the date of supply of copies of documents under Section 230
fourteen days from the date of framing of charge
explanation: Section 262(1) of the BNSS (old Section 239 CrPC) allows the accused to apply for discharge within sixty days from the date of supply of copies of documents under Section 230. If the Magistrate considers the charge groundless, he shall discharge the accused, recording his reasons (Section 262(2)).

subject: bnss
question: Under the proviso to Section 176(1) of the BNSS, the statement of a victim of rape shall be recorded:
options: only at the police station, by the officer in charge
only before a Judicial Magistrate in open court
by the Sessions Judge at the time of trial
at her residence or a place of her choice and, as far as practicable, by a woman police officer in the presence of her parents, guardian, near relatives or a local social worker
explanation: The proviso to Section 176(1) of the BNSS (old Section 157(1) proviso CrPC) requires the victim's statement in a rape case to be recorded at her residence or a place of her choice, as far as practicable by a woman police officer, in the presence of her parents, guardian, near relatives or a social worker of the locality. The BNSS adds that the statement may also be recorded through audio-video electronic means, including a mobile phone.

subject: bnss
question: No court shall take cognizance of an offence of contempt of the lawful authority of public servants (such as disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant) except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or his superior. This bar is in:
explanation: Section 215 of the BNSS (old Section 195 CrPC) bars cognizance of offences of contempt of the lawful authority of public servants, offences against public justice and offences relating to documents given in evidence, except on the written complaint of the public servant concerned (or his superior) or of the court concerned. Section 218 (old Section 197) concerns sanction to prosecute judges and public servants.

subject: bnss
question: The duty of every State Government, in coordination with the Central Government, to prepare a scheme for providing funds for compensation to victims of crime and their dependants is in:
explanation: Section 396 of the BNSS (old Section 357A CrPC) requires every State Government, in coordination with the Central Government, to prepare a victim compensation scheme, with the District or State Legal Services Authority deciding the quantum. Section 395 (old Section 357) deals with orders to pay compensation, Section 397 (old Section 357C) with free medical treatment of victims, and Section 398 with witness protection.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 397 of the BNSS, all hospitals, public or private, shall immediately provide first aid or medical treatment free of cost to victims of certain offences, including:
options: all offences punishable with more than three years
rape and acid attack offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
explanation: Section 397 of the BNSS (old Section 357C CrPC) requires all hospitals, whether run by the Central Government, State Government, local bodies or any other person, to provide first aid or medical treatment free of cost to victims of acid attack and of rape and related sexual offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and to inform the police immediately.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 403 of the BNSS, once a court has signed its judgment or final order disposing of a case, it shall not alter or review it, except:
options: to correct a clerical or arithmetical error, or as otherwise provided by the Sanhita or other law
on the application of the Public Prosecutor
with the consent of both parties
explanation: Section 403 of the BNSS (old Section 362 CrPC) bars a criminal court, after it has signed its judgment or final order, from altering or reviewing it except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error, save as otherwise provided by the Sanhita or any other law for the time being in force. The High Court's inherent power under Section 528 is not curtailed by it.

subject: bnss
question: A person accused of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life is generally not to be released on bail under Section 480(1) of the BNSS if there are reasonable grounds for believing him guilty. Under the proviso, the court may nevertheless direct release on bail if the person is:
options: a woman, or sick or infirm
a resident of the same district
explanation: Section 480(1) of the BNSS (old Section 437(1) CrPC) restricts bail by a court other than the High Court or Court of Session where there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused guilty of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment. Its proviso nevertheless allows the court to direct release on bail where the accused is, among others, a woman or sick or infirm.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 343 of the BNSS, a tender of pardon to an accomplice, on condition of his making a full and true disclosure, may be made in respect of:
options: any offence punishable with fine only
offences triable exclusively by a Court of Session or a Special Judge, or punishable with imprisonment extending to seven years or a more severe sentence
only offences in which the victim consents
explanation: Section 343 of the BNSS (old Section 306 CrPC) allows the Chief Judicial Magistrate at any stage of investigation, inquiry or trial, and a Magistrate of the first class during inquiry or trial, to tender pardon to an accomplice. It applies to offences triable exclusively by a Court of Session or Special Judge, and to offences punishable with imprisonment that may extend to seven years or with a more severe sentence.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 179(1) of the BNSS, which of the following persons shall NOT be required by a police officer to attend at any place other than the place where he or she resides?
options: A government employee summoned during office hours
A person accused of a cognizable offence
explanation: The proviso to Section 179(1) of the BNSS (old Section 160(1) CrPC) exempts a male person under fifteen or above sixty years of age, a woman, a mentally or physically disabled person, and a person with acute illness from being required to attend anywhere other than where they reside. The CrPC exemption applied to males above sixty-five; the BNSS lowered it to sixty and added persons with acute illness.

flags.note: Confirm the BNSS age thresholds (under 15, above 60) and the addition of 'acute illness' in the proviso to Section 179(1).

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 360 of the BNSS, which corresponds to Section 321 of the CrPC, before allowing the Public Prosecutor to withdraw from the prosecution of any person, the court must, under the new proviso:
options: obtain the sanction of the State Government
give an opportunity of being heard to the victim in the case
record the evidence of at least one witness
explanation: Section 360 of the BNSS carries forward the Public Prosecutor's power to withdraw from prosecution with the consent of the court before judgment. Its new proviso requires that no court shall allow such withdrawal without giving the victim in the case an opportunity of being heard.

flags.note: Confirm the wording of the victim-hearing proviso added to Section 360 BNSS.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 84(4) of the BNSS, where a person against whom a proclamation has been published fails to appear, the court may, after inquiry, declare him a proclaimed offender if he is accused of an offence:
options: punishable with imprisonment of three years or more
listed only in a schedule of specified IPC offences
punishable with imprisonment of ten years or more, imprisonment for life or death
of any kind, cognizable or non-cognizable
explanation: Section 84(4) of the BNSS (old Section 82(4) CrPC) permits a declaration as proclaimed offender where the person is accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment of ten years or more, life imprisonment or death under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or any other law. The CrPC instead listed specific sections of the IPC.

flags.note: Confirm that Section 84(4) BNSS uses the 'ten years or more, life or death' threshold in place of the CrPC's list of IPC sections.

subject: bnss
question: Under Section 144(1)(c) of the BNSS, a Magistrate may order a person with sufficient means to pay maintenance to his child who has attained majority only where that child:
options: is unemployed for more than one year
is, by reason of any physical or mental abnormality or injury, unable to maintain itself
explanation: Section 144(1)(c) of the BNSS (old Section 125(1)(c) CrPC) allows maintenance for a legitimate or illegitimate child, not being a married daughter, who has attained majority only where the child is unable to maintain itself by reason of any physical or mental abnormality or injury. Minor children are covered separately by clause (b).
